newsitem.title: USA: Asia owes fast growth to openness - Fed's McDonough.
newsitem.headline: Asia owes fast growth to openness - Fed's McDonough.

text.p: The rapidly-growing Asian "Tigers" owe much of their success to open markets and official efforts to restrain inflation, said New York Federal Reserve Bank President William McDonough.
Asia's economic powerhouses have used their broad ties to global markets for technology, capital and trading partners in turning in double-digit annual growth, said McDonough.

"They have crafted policies...that are consistent with the market-friendly approach which has played a fundamental role in the development process," said McDonough in a speech to the Hong Kong Monetary Authority.
A copy of McDonough's speech was released in New York.
McDonough praised Asian governments for their efforts to keep domestic inflation generally below 10 percent annually, despite meteoric economic growth over the last 30 years.
"By keeping inflation low, macroeconomic policies have enabled these economies to perform at or at least near, long-run potential output and productivity levels," he said.
The prolonged nature of the Asian economic surge highlights the durability of the Tiger phenomenon and suggests continued strong growth in Asia for years to come, the New York Fed president said.
"Asia's share in the world economy has risen considerably over the years, leaving no doubt that Asia's performance in the past three decades cannot be considered a flash in the pan," McDonough said.
While Hong Kong, Singapore, Taiwan and South Korea have led the rapid Asian expansion, China, Indonesia, Malaysia and Thailand have followed close behind over the last 20 years, McDonough noted.
The next potential Tigers appear to be Vietnam, India, the Phillipines and Cambodia, with each having worked to modernize its economy, McDonough said.
"Among the new reformers, Vietnam now appears to be showing signs of joining the ranks of high-growth economies," he added.
But China remains somewhat behind its neighbors in its efforts to fully open its fledgling market economy, McDonough said.

"Further structural changes will be required in both institutions and policies to firmly establish and maintain a market-friendly environment and to provide a sustainable, stable path for economic development" in China, he added.
